---
name: trail-write-gotchas
description: "entire trail write gotchas: body PATCH 503s at every size, labels are not writable, and probing safely needs a scratch trail with a branch"
metadata:
  type: reference
---

Gotchas when exercising `entire trail` **writes** against entire-api.

There is no backend switch to set: `ENTIRE_TRAILS_BACKEND` was removed on
2026-08-18 and entire-api is the only backend, so writes work by default. (The
old advice to export that var is dead — don't go looking for it.)

- **`trail update --body` 503s at every payload size.** Measured 2026-08-17 on
  trail #1017, 200 B through 4 KB, while `--title` PATCH, `trail create --body`,
  `trail show`, and `trail delete` all succeeded in the same minute. The body
  PATCH travels as its own request (`splitTrailUpdate` in `trail_cmd.go` — the
  server rejects body combined with metadata), so it fails in isolation. Not a
  size limit and not transient: retries across ~10 minutes never succeeded. A
  failed body PATCH leaves the existing body untouched, so retrying is safe.
- **Labels are read-only.** `--add-label`/`--remove-label` no longer exist; the
  API accepts no label writes. Reads (`trail show`'s `Labels:` line) still work.
- **Probing safely needs a scratch trail *with* a branch.** `trail update` can
  only target a trail **by branch**, so a `--no-branch` scratch trail is
  unpatchable — but creating one with `--branch` also **creates and pushes that
  branch to origin**. Clean up both the trail and the remote branch afterwards.

Related: [[trail-tune-command]], [[no-fluff-in-review-artifacts]]

Problem: Codex was the one agent named in the original subagent-tracking request with zero subagent tracking, despite shipping first-class hooks for it (SubagentStart/SubagentStop, schemas in codex-rs/hooks/schema/generated/) and despite multi_agent being stable/true since 0.147.
Solution: Wire both hooks. Codex's identity fields are the opposite of what the names suggest, and getting it backwards would attribute subagent work to a session Entire has never seen: session_id is "the identity shared by the root thread and all descendant threads" — the user's session — so it maps straight to SessionID, while agent_id is the subagent thread's own id. Codex sends no tool_use_id, so agent_id doubles as ToolUseID: it is the only value correlating a start with its stop, and Entire keys pre-task state (pre-task-<id>.json) and the task metadata directory on ToolUseID. SubagentStop carries two transcripts — transcript_path is the parent rollout, agent_transcript_path the subagent's own.
Rather than teach the framework a second layout to guess, Event.SubagentTranscriptPath lets an agent declare where its subagent transcript is; handleLifecycleSubagentEnd prefers it and falls back to the Claude Code layout guess. A declared-but-missing path warns rather than silently substituting, because that disagreement between contract and behaviour is exactly what went unnoticed while the guess quietly returned "" for every non-Claude agent.
That mechanism immediately fixes a second agent: Cursor has parsed agent_transcript_path into its raw struct all along and never forwarded it, so Cursor probed Claude Code's nested layout under Cursor's session directory, found nothing, and stored no subagent transcript — the same failure #1935 fixed for Claude Code. One line, plus a test.
Installer: both hooks go into .codex/hooks.json under PascalCase keys (SubagentStart/SubagentStop), matching Codex's own test fixtures — worth stating because HookEventName serializes snake_case elsewhere in Codex's protocol, and following that would have produced hooks that never fire. AreHooksInstalled now requires them, so a repo enabled before they existed reports drift and picks them up on the next install instead of silently tracking nothing. AGENT.md's two stale claims are corrected: hooks need no feature flag as of 0.147, and "No subagent hooks" is no longer true.

Fixed. The error wasn't a size limit or a flaky server — `entire trail update --body` was sending the description on the wrong route.

**What was happening:** `splitTrailUpdate` sent the body as its own `PATCH /trails/{host}/{owner}/{repo}/{number}` request (because the server rejects body+metadata combined). But that route never served body writes at all — it answers a `body` field with an unconditional 503, and since the API redacts 5xx messages, callers only ever saw "Service Unavailable". Your pasted text is that redacted message's real cause.

**The fix** (`cmd/entire/cli/trail_cmd.go`, `cmd/entire/cli/api/trail_types.go`):

- New `sendTrailBody` issues `PUT <trail path>/body` with `{"markdown": ..., "overwrite": true}`.
- `overwrite: true` is required: without it the route 409s (`document_not_empty`) against any trail that already has a description — i.e. every edit except a first write. The interactive path already shows the current description before you edit it, and `--body` is an explicit replacement, so replace-semantics is what the command already meant.
- `api.TrailUpdateRequest` lost its `Body` field entirely, so the metadata PATCH can no longer carry a body. `splitTrailUpdate` is gone — `buildTrailUpdateRequest` now returns the metadata request plus the new description separately, so the wrong-route mistake isn't representable. `markdown` carries no `omitempty`, which is what keeps `--body=` (clear the description) working.
- `--body`'s help now reads "Replace the description (`--body=` clears it)".
- Metadata + body still go out as two requests and still aren't atomic; the existing "metadata was updated, but the body update failed" error is unchanged.

**Verification:** unit tests rewritten to model the real routing (PATCH refuses a body, PUT `/body` accepts `{markdown, overwrite}`); `mise run fmt && mise run lint` clean; `mise run test:ci` fully green. I also confirmed read-only against the live cell's OpenAPI that `PUT /trails/{host}/{owner}/{repo}/{number}/body` exists with exactly the `markdown`/`contentJson`/`overwrite` shape being sent.

One gap: I haven't done a live end-to-end write. `trail update` targets a trail by branch, and this branch has no trail, so verifying for real means creating a scratch trail with `--branch` — which also creates and pushes that branch to origin. <result>Read the diff and the surrounding code (`trail_cmd.go`, `api/trail_types.go`, all 24 `checkTrailResponse` call sites, the `trail*Path` helpers, and the trail test fixtures). Two findings worth acting on; the other two questions come back clean.

## Findings

**1. `cmd/entire/cli/api/trail_types.go:176` — `TrailBodyResponse` is a second Go type for a server entity the package already models: `TrailBodyDocument`.**
`TrailBodyDocument` (same file, line 89, doc comment: "the trail's description editor document") already models the body document on the read path, keyed on the same `textSnapshot` field, and is reached as `TrailResource.BodyDocument` (line 79) by `fetchTrailDescription` (`trail_cmd.go:435-451`). The PUT `.../body` response is the same document, just fuller. Use instead: either decode the PUT response into `api.TrailBodyDocument`, or extend `TrailBodyDocument` with `ID`/`DocumentKey`/`UpdatedAt` and share it between `TrailResource.BodyDocument` and the write path. Cost of not reusing: one server concept now has two Go types, so a later feature that wants to show the written-back snapshot or `updatedAt` has to pick one, and a server rename of `textSnapshot` (or an added field) needs both edited — with nothing in either doc comment pointing at the other. Note the cheaper alternative the file already contains: `deleteTrailByNumber` (`trail_cmd.go:1879-1887`) ends at `return checkTrailResponse(resp)` when nothing reads the body, which is exactly `sendTrailBody`'s situation — taking that route deletes the new type outright.

**2. `cmd/entire/cli/trail_cmd.go:1646` — `path+"/body"` inlines a subresource route instead of adding the `trail*Path` helper every other trail subresource has.**
The convention is one named helper per subresource, all built the same way: `trailApprovalsPath` (`trail_approval_cmd.go:16` → `trailNumberPath(...) + "/approvals"`), `trailThreadsPath` / `trailThreadPath` / `trailThreadMessagesPath` (`trail_comment_cmd.go:21-34`). Use instead: add `trailBodyPath(forge, owner, repo string, number int)` next to `trailNumberPath` (`trail_cmd.go:2133-2138`) and pass the finished path into `sendTrailBody`. Cost of not reusing: `sendTrailBody`'s `path` parameter means something different from its sibling `sendTrailPatch`'s (parent trail vs. the actual route written to), so the two adjacent helpers can't be read the same way; and the body route is invisible to a grep over the other trail route helpers — the one place route knowledge is currently centralized, in a change whose whole point is which route the body goes to.

## Checked, nothing to flag

- **`sendTrailBody` vs `sendTrailPatch` (and the wider send/check/decode pattern).** No generic helper exists to call. All 24 `checkTrailResponse` sites (`trail_comment_cmd.go`, `trail_approval_cmd.go`, `trail_review_cmd.go:1020-1435`, `trail_watch_cmd.go`, `trail_cmd.go`) open-code the same four steps; the `api` package offers only the primitives (`DecodeJSON`, `CheckResponse`, `Put`/`Patch`). `sendTrailBody` follows the established pattern rather than inventing one. Collapsing it and `sendTrailPatch` into one generic helper would be a *new* abstraction (they differ in verb, route, and decode target, and `Client` exposes no method-taking JSON call — `doJSON` is private), not reuse of an existing one, so I'm not asking for it. Fixing finding 1 via the `deleteTrailByNumber` shape shrinks the overlap to ~6 lines anyway.
- **Tests.** The new `record` closure and `trailWrite` struct have no existing counterpart to reuse: `coreRecorder` (`logout_test.go:332`) is entire-core-specific and `trailShowTestServer` (`trail_cmd_test.go:1537`) only serves the show path. The repeated list-response stanza in the update tests predates this diff and no new copy was added. Worth noting only in passing: `TestRunTrailUpdateSendsTitleAsPatchAndBodyAsPut` (line 2035) and `TestRunTrailUpdateReportsAppliedMetadataWhenBodyWriteFails` (line 2166) now each hard-code the same three-route layout, so a future route change is a two-place edit — but their PUT behaviours diverge deliberately (record-and-succeed vs. 503), and a shared fixture would need a parameter for exactly that, so I'd leave it.</result>

## Findings (simplification only)

**1. `cmd/entire/cli/trail_cmd.go:1550` — the second return value is pure pass-through of state the only caller already holds.**
`buildTrailUpdateRequest` does not transform the description at all (no trim, no merge — unlike `Type`/`Assignees`); it just copies `inputs.Body` behind a pointer when `inputs.BodyChanged`. At the call site both halves are already in scope: `body` (local, line 1342, re-assigned by the interactive form at 1385) and `inputs.BodyChanged` (recomputed at 1394). Simpler: keep the single return, stop passing `Body`/`BodyChanged` into it, and write

```go
if inputs.BodyChanged {
    if err := sendTrailBody(ctx, client, path, body); err != nil { ... }
}
```

The `*string` also stops being needed the moment the bool is used directly — absent-vs-empty stays exactly as load-bearing, carried by `BodyChanged` instead of by nil. This deletes the `var newBody *string`, the `body := inputs.Body; newBody = &body` copy at 1561 (inconsistent with `req.Status = &inputs.Status` two lines up, which is safe because `inputs` is a value parameter), the `req, _ :=` churn in three tests, and collapses `TestBuildTrailUpdateRequestCanClearBody` + the body half of `TestBuildTrailUpdateRequestSeparatesBodyFromMetadata` into the flag check they actually assert. Cost of the current form: a maintainer reading `runTrailUpdateWithClient` has to hold two representations of "did the body change" (`inputs.BodyChanged` and `newBody != nil`) and trust they never disagree.

**2. `cmd/entire/cli/trail_cmd.go:1585-1606` — the reflective `trailUpdateRequestHasFields` (plus its 30-line reflective table test) is replaceable by one comparison.** Every field of `api.TrailUpdateRequest` is a pointer, so the struct is comparable: `hasMeta := updateReq != (api.TrailUpdateRequest{})`. I confirmed by compiling and running it against the real type — zero equals zero, and a pointer-to-empty-string counts as set, i.e. byte-identical semantics to the `IsZero` loop. It also keeps the property the long comment is defending, more firmly: a future non-pointer *slice* field makes the struct non-comparable and the line stops compiling, forcing the author to decide, where reflection silently absorbs it. That removes the helper, its two paragraphs of comment, and `TestTrailUpdateRequestCountsEveryFieldAsMetadata` (whose reason to exist — "reflection might get a field wrong" — is gone, including its `require.NotZero` vacuity guard and its `field.Type.Kind() == reflect.Ptr` assertion). Cost today: ~45 lines of reflection across prod and test to compute something the language computes with `!=`.

**3. `cmd/entire/cli/api/trail_types.go:176-181` and `trail_cmd.go:1654` — `TrailBodyResponse`'s four fields are decoded and thrown away, and the comment justifying them is not accurate.** Nothing reads `ID`/`DocumentKey`/`TextSnapshot`/`UpdatedAt` (grep: only the fake server in the test constructs it). The stated job — "distinguishes the documented response from an unrelated 200 (a proxy's HTML, say)" — is done by *any* JSON decode, not by these fields: `json.Unmarshal` neither requires them to be present nor rejects unknown ones, so `{}` and the real document are indistinguishable to this check. Simpler: `var ignored struct{}` (or `api.DecodeJSON(resp, &struct{}{})`) in `sendTrailBody` with a one-line "only checks the 200 really is JSON", and drop the exported type; the test's `api.TrailBodyResponse{...}` literal becomes a plain map like the rejection literals next to it. Cost: a new exported API type plus a 4-line justification a maintainer must re-derive to discover it guarantees nothing.

**4. `cmd/entire/cli/trail_cmd_test.go:1284-1291` — `TestTrailBodyRequestMarshalsAnEmptyMarkdown` earns its place, but not at four statements.** The property (no `omitempty` on `Markdown`) is project-owned, not stdlib, so keep the test; the marshal → unmarshal-into-`map[string]any` → compare-map round trip is the part testing `encoding/json`. Simpler:

```go
data, err := json.Marshal(api.TrailBodyRequest{Markdown: "", Overwrite: true})
require.NoError(t, err)
require.JSONEq(t, `{"markdown":"","overwrite":true}`, string(data))
```

Cost of the current form: the `map[string]any{...: true}` literal makes the reader reconstruct the wire shape mentally instead of reading it.

**5. `cmd/entire/cli/trail_cmd_test.go:2048` — the `record` closure is worth keeping, but its signature carries two things it does not need.** The `t *testing.T` parameter shadows the `t` the closure already captures (it is defined inside the test), and the `bool` return exists only so both call sites can write `if !ok { return }`. Simpler: `record := func(r *http.Request) map[string]any` returning nil on a decode error, so callers read `got := record(r); if got == nil { return }` — and the PUT branch, which discards the map entirely, becomes `record(r)`. The `trailWrite` struct plus the single `require.Equal` on `[]trailWrite` is the right amount of machinery: it replaces two duplicated decode+lock blocks and pins method, path, and exact body in one readable literal.

**6. `cmd/entire/cli/trail_cmd_test.go:42-45 — `trailBodyField` is now a one-use constant.** The diff removed its second call site, leaving only the `got[trailBodyField]` guard at line 2076. Inline `got["body"]` and move the "this must never appear on the metadata PATCH" sentence to the guard, where the reader is. Cost: a name + three-line comment at the top of the file that a maintainer must jump to in order to learn it means the literal `"body"`.

Nothing else in the diff struck me as over-built: `sendTrailBody` mirrors `sendTrailPatch`'s shape, the `hasMeta`/`newBody` two-request block keeps its original nesting, and the long comments are explanatory rather than restating the code.</result>

**No meaningful efficiency waste in this diff.** The change is, if anything, a small net reduction in work: the deleted `splitTrailUpdate` did a full `api.TrailUpdateRequest` struct copy plus two heap allocations (`b := *full.Body`, `&api.TrailUpdateRequest{Body: &b}`) on every invocation; the replacement does one 16-byte allocation. ### Findings

**1. `/Users/soph/.herdr/worktrees/cli/soph-trail-body-api-fix/cmd/entire/cli/trail_cmd.go:1654` — `sendTrailBody` decodes `TrailBodyResponse` and discards every field, and `textSnapshot` is the description it just sent, echoed back.**
Cheaper: skip the `DecodeJSON` and let `defer resp.Body.Close()` handle it, or `io.Copy(io.Discard, resp.Body)` if the drain is what you want. **Theoretical.** `api.DecodeJSON` already reads the body to completion (`io.ReadAll` under a 16 MB limit), so the connection is fully drained exactly as it is at every other write call site in the repo (`trail_approval_cmd.go:81`, `trail_comment_cmd.go:341`, `trail_review_cmd.go:1428`) — the new code matches that convention, and connection reuse is moot anyway since this is the last request of a one-shot process. The only true waste is one `json.Unmarshal` plus four discarded string headers over a few KB, once per `trail update`.

**2. `/Users/soph/.herdr/worktrees/cli/soph-trail-body-api-fix/cmd/entire/cli/trail_cmd.go:1453` and `:1458` — the metadata PATCH and body PUT are strictly sequential but have no data dependency, so they *could* be concurrent.**
The PUT's path comes from `found.Number` (already in hand at 1442), and because `Overwrite: true` is used instead of `If-Match`, nothing from the PATCH response feeds the PUT. An `errgroup` would save one RTT. **Measurable in wall clock (one RTT, ~50–300 ms) but not worth doing.** The command has already spent one-to-two RTTs before reaching here (`findTrailByBranch`'s list paging, plus the interactive detail GET), so it's a fraction of total latency for a human-invoked command; and the sequence is what makes the deliberate partial-state message at 1459-1461 ("metadata was updated, but the body update failed") true — concurrency would replace one precise message with two possible failures and no ordering guarantee. Keep it sequential.

**3. `/Users/soph/.herdr/worktrees/cli/soph-trail-body-api-fix/cmd/entire/cli/trail_cmd.go:444` — the interactive-only detail GET decodes the full trail resource through `decodeNormalizedTrailJSON`, which is three passes over the document (unmarshal into `any`, reflective map rebuild, re-marshal, unmarshal into `TrailResource`) to extract one string.**
Pre-existing, not introduced here, but it sits on this command path. If the route the diff establishes also serves `GET .../{number}/body`, fetching that instead would return and decode only the body document (and would bypass `TrailResource.UnmarshalJSON` entirely, since `TrailBodyResponse` has no custom unmarshaler). **Theoretical** — `TrailResource` is flat with no nested collections, so three passes over a few KB is microseconds; and I cannot confirm from this repo that the route serves GET.

Worth stating for the record on the question you raised: **the detail GET does not overlap with anything the body write needs.** It exists only to seed the interactive form (the list resource omits `bodyDocument`), it is skipped entirely when `--body` is passed non-interactively, and the write consumes nothing from it — so there is no round trip to eliminate by reordering or merging the two.

**4. `/Users/soph/.herdr/worktrees/cli/soph-trail-body-api-fix/cmd/entire/cli/trail_cmd.go:1620` — same discarded decode as #1 in `sendTrailPatch`, but strictly more expensive, because `TrailUpdateResponse` embeds `TrailResource` and so routes through the three-pass normalizer.**
Unchanged by the diff; listed only because #1 was modeled on it and inherited the pattern. **Theoretical**, same magnitude reasoning as #3.

### Explicitly not findings

- **`trail_cmd.go:1561` (`body := inputs.Body; newBody = &body`)** — this copies a 16-byte string header, not character data; Go strings share their backing array. It happens once per command. The alternative `&inputs.Body` is not cheaper — `inputs` already escapes to the heap via `req.Status = &inputs.Status` at 1552.
- **The `record` closure in `trail_cmd_test.go`** — it captures `mu` and `writes` by reference (they escape to the heap), exactly as the inline handler code it replaces already did, and its lifetime is the `httptest` server's, i.e. one test. It correctly takes `*testing.T` as a parameter rather than capturing it. No cost worth naming.
- **Startup / hot paths** — nothing added. `sendTrailBody` is reachable only from `trail update`; no package-level state, no `init()`, no new work on any hook path.</result>

<result>## Verdict on the altitude questions

**Command-layer routing is the right depth.** I grepped the whole repo: `api.TrailUpdateRequest` is referenced only in `trail_cmd.go` and `api/trail_types.go`; there are exactly five `client.Patch`/`client.Put` call sites and the other three write review-comment and thread-message bodies, not descriptions. The `api` package deliberately holds no trail write helpers at all — the only trail method on `*api.Client` is the read probe `TrailsEnabled` (`/Users/soph/.herdr/worktrees/cli/soph-trail-body-api-fix/cmd/entire/cli/api/trails.go:13`) — and every trail route in the CLI is spelled at the command layer (`trailNumberPath` at `trail_cmd.go:2130`, `trailThreadPath` in `trail_comment_cmd.go`, `trailReviewCommentPath` at `trail_review_cmd.go:1126`). The one thing that *must* be shared to stop this recurring — the absence of a `Body` field on `api.TrailUpdateRequest` — is in the `api` package, so a future caller cannot re-make the mistake. Right split.

**No second caller, verified against the server.** The only other description write is `trail create`'s POST `body` field (`trail_cmd.go:1200`), and the server does serve it: `resolveTrailCreate` converts it with `editorjson.MarkdownToEditorJSON` and seeds the body document (`~/Work/entire/devenv/entire-api/internal/httpapi/trails_write.go:1198-1206`). `.entire/runners/trail-summary.json` declares `trail_field: "body"`, but that runner executes in entire-api, not this CLI. Nothing in `cmd/entire/cli/review/`, `review_bridge.go`, `trail_review_cmd.go`, `trail_comment_cmd.go`, runner/dispatch/MCP code, integration tests, or e2e writes a trail description.

**Removing `Body` from `TrailUpdateRequest` pushes nothing onto callers.** The single caller already had to know about two requests — `splitTrailUpdate` existed precisely for that — so this swaps two PATCHes for a PATCH plus a PUT and gains a compile-time guard. Correct generalization.

## Findings

**1. `overwrite: true` is hardcoded where no caller can choose it, and it is the only unconditional clobber of a trail body in the platform.** `/Users/soph/.herdr/worktrees/cli/soph-trail-body-api-fix/cmd/entire/cli/trail_cmd.go:1645`

The server built the safe path specifically for this caller: `trailBodyNotEmptyError` attaches the current ETag as a real response header on the 409 because, per its own doc, "this response is the only place they can ever learn it" (`entire-api/internal/httpapi/trails_body_write.go:95-98`), and the route's `If-Match` doc states "a MATCHING If-Match also satisfies the non-empty-document guard on its own — overwrite:true is not needed alongside it" (`trails_body_write.go:58`). So the diff's justification at `trail_cmd.go:1636-1643` ("the route's If-Match alternative cannot be used… its ETag is only ever handed out by this route's own response header") is inverted: the 409 is exactly the handout, engineered for a caller with no platform grant. The platform's *other* body writer takes the opposite policy — entire-api's runner (the one driven by `trail-summary.json`) writes `OnlyIfEmpty: true` (`entire-api/internal/runner/trailbody.go:165`) under the standing rule "an unwritten body stays seedable while a wrongly written one does not — so uncertainty skips."

Deeper place: overwrite/If-Match is per-write policy, so it belongs with the caller — a parameter on `sendTrailBody`, or a small write helper that tries without overwrite and uses the 409's ETag. The explicit `--body` flag can pass unconditional; the interactive path at `trail_cmd.go:1367`, which prefills a form from a read and is a textbook read-modify-write, should not.

Cost of leaving it: every CLI description write is an unconditional clobber with the server's guard disabled and no way for any caller to opt in. A description edited in the web editor while the interactive form is open is destroyed with no error, and the first CLI `--body` write permanently switches the `trail-summary` runner to `document_not_empty` skips for that trail.

**2. Three hand-copied restatements of the server contract that the server's own commit already contradicts.** `cmd/entire/cli/api/trail_types.go:134-140`, `cmd/entire/cli/trail_cmd.go:1636-1643`, `cmd/entire/cli/trail_cmd_test.go:2077`

The PUT `.../body` route this change targets and the 503→400 change landed in the *same* entire-api commit (`7be4c69d`, "feat(httpapi): a trail-body write endpoint a person can actually reach", 2026-08-19, on `main`). `validateUpdateTrailBody` now returns 400 with the message served verbatim, with a comment saying 503 "was wrong twice over… useCompactErrors redacts every 5xx, so the one thing the caller needed… was the one thing it could not see" (`entire-api/internal/httpapi/trails_write.go:355-363`). Consequence: no deployment can serve the PUT and still 503 the PATCH body field, so the new end-to-end test at `trail_cmd_test.go:2077` pins the CLI against a server that cannot exist, and two doc comments state a transient status code as permanent fact.

Deeper place: pin the invariant (the metadata route carries no description; the type has no field) and let the server's actionable message reach the user — `api.CheckResponse` already surfaces it (`cmd/entire/cli/api/client.go:337-347`). Drop the status code and redaction story from the prose and from the fake handler's rejection.

Cost: a doc comment that reads authoritative and is wrong the day it lands, and a test whose name promises "routes trail writes exactly as production does" while encoding the opposite.

**3. The two-route plan is spread across four places in the command instead of being one value.** `cmd/entire/cli/trail_cmd.go:1550` (returns `(api.TrailUpdateRequest, *string)`), `:1444` (reflective `hasMeta`), `:1611` and `:1644` (two send helpers), with the route itself spelled inline as `path+"/body"` while every sibling trail route has a named builder near `:2130`.

A function called `buildTrailUpdateRequest` now returns a request plus a loose out-of-band pointer, and the "is there anything to send / what partially landed" logic lives at the call site as three conditionals.

Deeper place: one `trailUpdatePlan{meta api.TrailUpdateRequest; body *string}` with an `apply` that owns the ordering, the no-op case, and the partial-failure message — plus a `trailBodyPath` builder alongside `trailNumberPath`, which is also where the server's `/repos/{repo_id}/trails/{number}/body` twin would land if the CLI ever needs ID addressing.

Cost is modest but real: a third description-adjacent route, or the `--overwrite` decision from finding 1, means touching build, run, and both send helpers again rather than one plan type.</result>

The cleanup pass is done. Four agents reviewed in parallel; I applied six findings and skipped four.

**Applied**

1. **Duplicate type removed** (reuse + simplification + efficiency all landed here). `api.TrailBodyResponse` was a second Go type for a server entity the package already models — the body PUT returns the same document `TrailBodyDocument` models on the read path. Deleted it; `sendTrailBody` decodes into `api.TrailBodyDocument`. Its old justification comment ("distinguishes the documented response from an unrelated 200") was also false — any JSON decode does that — so it now says what it actually buys: confirms the 200 was JSON, drains the body.
2. **`trailBodyPath` helper** added next to `trailNumberPath`, matching the convention every other trail subresource follows (`trailApprovalsPath`, `trailThreadsPath`). The route is no longer spelled inline as `path+"/body"`, and `sendTrailBody`'s `path` parameter now means the same thing as its sibling `sendTrailPatch`'s.
3. **Dropped the second return value.** `buildTrailUpdateRequest` is back to one return; the call site uses the `body` local and `inputs.BodyChanged` it already holds. That removes two representations of "did the description change" (`newBody != nil` vs `inputs.BodyChanged`) that a maintainer had to trust never disagree, plus the `*string` and its local copy.
4. **Status codes out of prose and tests.** Altitude flagged my comments as pinning a redacted 503 that's changing. I checked: `origin/main` still returns 503, but there's uncommitted work in the entire-api tree switching it to a 400 with the message served verbatim — which is how you saw the real text at all. So the comments and the test now assert the invariant (the metadata route carries no description) and deliberately don't model a status code. The routing test's PATCH handler `t.Errorf`s if a description ever appears, which is stronger than mimicking a rejection.
5. **Better coverage for `--body=`** (clearing). Two vacuous unit tests (`…CanClearBody`, `…SeparatesBodyFromMetadata` — both testing a function that no longer touches the description) and the stdlib-ish marshal test are replaced by one end-to-end test that drives the real path and asserts the PUT carries `{"markdown":"","overwrite":true}`. That covers both silent-failure modes: gating on the flag rather than on non-empty text, and `omitempty` dropping the field.
6. **Test tidying:** one-use `trailBodyField` constant inlined, `record` closure simplified to return the map (no shadowed `t`, no `bool`).

**Skipped**

- **Replacing reflective `trailUpdateRequestHasFields` with `req != (api.TrailUpdateRequest{})`** — correct and would delete ~45 lines, but that mechanism and its table test predate this change; my diff didn't add that complexity. Worth a separate pass if you want it.
- **Parameterizing `overwrite`** (altitude's top finding). The reasoning was partly inverted: the ETag you get from the 409 is the refusal you just triggered, so retrying with it clobbers exactly as `overwrite` does, one round trip later — it isn't a compare-and-set. Real safety needs the ETag of the document the user read, which no trail read provides. Giving users the choice is a new flag, not a cleanup; I rewrote the comment to say that plainly instead.
- **Running the PATCH and PUT concurrently** — the efficiency agent recommended against it itself: it saves one RTT on a human-invoked command and would break the precise "metadata applied, body didn't" error.
- **A `trailUpdatePlan` struct with an `apply` method** — more machinery than a one-caller, 15-line block needs, and it pulls against the simplification above.

fix(trail): write descriptions through the body route, not the metadata PATCH

`entire trail update --body` sent the description as a `body` field on
PATCH /api/v1/trails/{host}/{owner}/{repo}/{number}. That route does not
serve body writes at all: it rejects the field and names the dedicated
route to use instead. Because the rejection has been served as a redacted
5xx, the caller only ever saw a bare "Service Unavailable" — so this read
as a flaky server, and was measured across payload sizes and retried over
ten minutes before anyone suspected the route was simply wrong.

Route the description to PUT .../{number}/body instead, with
{"markdown": ..., "overwrite": true}. Overwrite is what makes editing an
existing description work: left false the route refuses any non-empty
description with 409 document_not_empty, i.e. every write except the
first. It also matches what --body already means — the interactive path
shows the current description before you edit it. Its If-Match
alternative is not a substitute: that ETag is only handed out by a body
write's own response, so obtaining one means being refused and retrying,
which clobbers exactly as overwrite does a round trip later.

api.TrailUpdateRequest loses its Body field entirely, so sending a
description on the metadata route is no longer representable, and
splitTrailUpdate — which existed only to send the body as its own PATCH —
goes with it. Metadata and description still travel as two non-atomic
requests, and the existing "metadata was updated, but the body update
failed" error is unchanged.

The route and its request shape were verified against the deployed cell's
OpenAPI, not just the server source: PUT
/trails/{host}/{owner}/{repo}/{number}/body accepts markdown/contentJson
plus overwrite. No status code is pinned in the CLI's comments or tests —
the rejection has been a redacted 5xx and is moving to a 4xx, and the CLI
must behave the same either way.
